title: Ancient Najd
subtitle: 1,200–300 BC · The Camel Nomads, the Arab Queens, the Kingdom of Qedar and the Oases of al-Yamama

categories.label: Power
categories.subtitle: Central Arabia enters the written record as a frontier of tribes — the camel nomads the Assyrians called ʿAribi, five ruling queens, the confederation of Qedar, and the oasis farmers of al-Yamama

entries.group: The Camel Nomads and the ʿAribi (853–700 BC)
entries.label: Gindibu the Arab, and the first 'Arabs'
entries.loc: Qarqar, Syria · Gindibu of the Najd steppe
entries.hint: At the battle of Qarqar, Shalmaneser III's annal lists 'Gindibu the Aribi' contributing 1,000 camels to the coalition against Assyria. It is the earliest datable use of the name 'Arab' and the first appearance of the camel as a military asset of the plateau tribes.
entries.note: the Kurkh Monolith of Shalmaneser III (853 BC); Israel Ephʿal, 'The Ancient Arabs: Nomads on the Borders of the Fertile Crescent 9th–5th Centuries B.C.' (1982).

entries.group: The Camel Nomads and the ʿAribi (853–700 BC)
entries.label: The ʿAribi on the Assyrian tribute frontier
entries.loc: the desert edge of Najd, toward Assyria
entries.hint: From Tiglath-Pileser III onward the Assyrians extracted tribute — camels, aromatics, gold — from a shifting set of 'Arab' tribal leaders on the steppe, with the Najd plateau behind them as the zone of raiding and of refuge no army could reach.
entries.note: the Assyrian royal annals (Tiglath-Pileser III, Sargon II, Sennacherib); Ephʿal (1982).

entries.group: The Arab Queens of the Assyrian Records (738–690 BC)
entries.label: The Arab queens
entries.hint: The Assyrian annals name five women — Zabibe, Samsi, Yatiʿe, Teʾelkhunu and Tabua — as rulers of North Arabian tribal confederations, taking tribute, fielding armies and, in Tabua's case, raised at the Assyrian court and installed as queen.
entries.note: the annals of Tiglath-Pileser III, Sargon II and Sennacherib; Ephʿal (1982); Nadav Naʾaman on the Arab queens.

entries.group: The Arab Queens of the Assyrian Records (738–690 BC)
entries.label: Adummatu, the desert stronghold
entries.hint: The great oasis of Adummatu controlled the northern gate of the plateau and held the images of the tribal gods. Sennacherib sacked it around 688 BC and carried the gods and the priestess-queen Teʾelkhunu to Nineveh; Esarhaddon later returned them with the new queen Tabua.
entries.note: Sennacherib's and Esarhaddon's inscriptions on Adummatu; the Saudi–Italian excavations at Dumat al-Jandal (Charloux, al-Malki).

entries.group: The Kingdom of Qedar (7th–4th c BC)
entries.label: The kingdom of Qedar
entries.loc: from the Egyptian border to Dumah and the northern Najd
entries.hint: Qedar was the largest North Arabian tribal kingdom — a confederation held together by control of the caravan routes and the wells rather than by a fixed capital. Its kings, from Hazael and Uaite to Qainu, ranged across the whole northern desert.
entries.note: the Assyrian and biblical references to Qedar; Ephʿal (1982); the Qedarite dedications from Dumah and the eastern Delta.

entries.group: The Kingdom of Qedar (7th–4th c BC)
entries.label: Gashmu the Arabian, king of Qedar
entries.loc: the northern Najd and the routes to the Levant
entries.hint: Geshem — Gashmu — the Arabian opposed Nehemiah's rebuilding of Jerusalem's wall. A silver bowl from the eastern Nile Delta names 'Qainu son of Gashmu, king of Qedar', showing the kingdom at its height, dominating the trade from Arabia to the Mediterranean.
entries.note: Nehemiah 2:19, 6:1–6; the Tell el-Maskhuta silver bowls (Brooklyn Museum); William Dumbrell, 'The Tell el-Maskhuta bowls and the Kingdom of Qedar' (1971).

entries.group: The Oases of al-Yamama and the Interior
entries.label: Al-Yamama — the oases of Wadi Hanifa
entries.loc: Wadi Hanifa, al-Kharj and al-Aflaj, Saudi Arabia
entries.hint: The belt of springs and palm groves along Wadi Hanifa (the future Riyadh region) and at al-Kharj and al-Aflaj supported settled farming communities on the eastern edge of the plateau, remembered in Arab tradition as the land of the vanished tribes Tasm and Jadis.
entries.note: the Saudi Commission for Tourism and National Heritage surveys of al-Yamama and al-Kharj; the Arab genealogical tradition on Tasm and Jadis.

entries.label: The homeland of Kindah
entries.loc: Wadi al-Dawasir, southern Najd, Saudi Arabia
entries.hint: The tribe of Kindah, later royal, held its traditional homeland in the Wadi al-Dawasir country of the southern plateau, astride the route between Yemen and the Gulf. The central-Arabian tribal map that the classical and Islamic sources describe takes its shape in this period.
entries.note: the Arabic genealogical tradition on Kindah; the pre-Islamic South Arabian inscriptions mentioning Kdt (Kindah); Christian Robin on Kindah's origins.

categories.label: Conflict
categories.subtitle: The Assyrian frontier — Qarqar, the sack of Adummatu, the punitive columns into the desert — and the endless internal warfare of the raid and the well

entries.label: Qarqar and the camel contingent
entries.hint: Gindibu's thousand camels fought in the great western coalition that checked Shalmaneser III at Qarqar — the plateau tribes' first recorded appearance on a battlefield, as mobile auxiliaries to the settled kingdoms.
entries.note: the Kurkh Monolith; Ephʿal (1982).

entries.label: The punitive campaigns into the desert
entries.hint: Tiglath-Pileser defeated Samsi, Sennacherib sacked Adummatu, and Esarhaddon and Ashurbanipal marched columns deep into the sands against Uaite and Qedar. Each campaign claimed victory; each was followed by the tribes drifting back.
entries.note: the annals of the four kings; Ashurbanipal's account of the pursuit of Uaite through the desert (Prism A).

entries.label: The raid, the camel and the well
entries.hint: The internal warfare of the plateau was the ghazw — the raid for camels and for control of the wells and the pasture. Outside empires could disrupt it for a season but never end it; it was the plateau's normal politics.
entries.note: reconstructed from the later Arabic tradition of the ayyam al-ʿArab and from the rock inscriptions; Ephʿal (1982) on the pattern in the Assyrian period.

entries.label: Qedar and its rivals
entries.loc: the northern desert and the caravan routes
entries.hint: The Qedarite kings fought the ancestors of the Nabataeans, the Idumaeans and the other confederations for the wells and the caravan routes of the northern desert — the competition that Qedar, for a century, won.
entries.note: Ephʿal (1982); Robert Hoyland, 'Arabia and the Arabs' (2001), on the late Qedarite period.

categories.label: Order
categories.subtitle: An outside power's first administration of central-Arabian affairs, the confederation as a form of statehood, and the custody of the gods as the constitution of the desert polity

entries.label: Tribute, hostage and overseer on the frontier
entries.hint: Assyria governed the 'Arabs' through fixed tribute quotas, installed leaders like Tabua and Uaite, hostages held at Nineveh, and a resident overseer (qēpu). It is the first documented administration of central-Arabian affairs by an outside power.
entries.note: the Assyrian frontier correspondence; Ephʿal (1982) on the administrative apparatus.

entries.label: The confederation as a state
entries.loc: the northern Najd and the steppe
entries.hint: Qedar and the queens' polities held together through shared cult, marriage alliance and collective control of routes and wells, with no bureaucracy and no fixed capital — a distinct North Arabian model of political order that later Arab states would inherit.
entries.note: Ephʿal (1982); Hoyland, 'Arabia and the Arabs' (2001).

entries.label: Custody of the gods
entries.hint: Whoever held Adummatu held the images of the tribal gods, and control of the sanctuary conferred authority over the confederation. Sennacherib understood this well enough to carry the gods off, and Esarhaddon to send them back with a client queen.
entries.note: Esarhaddon's inscription on returning the gods of the Arabs; Ephʿal (1982).

categories.label: Belief
categories.subtitle: The gods the Assyrians listed by name when they looted the desert sanctuary, the standing stones of the wells, and the truce-shrine at Dumah that prefigures the pre-Islamic haram

entries.label: The North Arabian pantheon
entries.loc: across the plateau and the steppe
entries.hint: The gods Sennacherib took from Adummatu — Atarsamain, Nuhay, Ruldaiu, Abirillu, Atarquruma — and the goddess (han-)ʾIlat, Allat, are named in the Assyrian and later inscriptions as the deities of the desert tribes, an astral and warrior pantheon.
entries.note: Esarhaddon's list of the returned Arab gods; Hoyland, 'Arabia and the Arabs' (2001), on the North Arabian pantheon.

entries.label: The standing stone and the well
entries.loc: the route junctions of the plateau
entries.hint: Aniconic standing stones and open-air sanctuaries clustered at wells and where routes met; the Assyrian texts' apkallatu — priestess — was a keeper of such a cult. It is the same betyl tradition seen in the northwest oases and, far south, in Yemen.
entries.note: Hoyland (2001); the betyl continuity is discussed across the Arabian religious literature.

entries.label: The truce-shrine at Dumah
entries.hint: Adummatu served the northern confederations as a place of pilgrimage and of truce, where feud was suspended and the gods of many tribes were kept together — the model for the haram sanctuaries that structured pre-Islamic Arabian society.
entries.note: Ephʿal (1982); the parallel to Mecca's later haram is drawn in Hoyland (2001) and Peters, 'The Hajj' (1994).

categories.label: Expression
categories.subtitle: The interior's own vast body of rock writing and rock art — names, genealogies, prayers, camels, horsemen and tribal brands

entries.label: The Ancient North Arabian inscriptions
entries.hint: Tens of thousands of short rock graffiti in the Thamudic scripts cover Najd — signatures, genealogies, prayers to the gods, records of travel, mourning and love. They are the everyday writing of a largely nomadic society, and most postdate this folio's start but begin within it.
entries.note: the OCIANA (Online Corpus of the Inscriptions of Ancient North Arabia) database; M. C. A. Macdonald on the Ancient North Arabian scripts.

entries.label: The rock art of Najd
entries.hint: Pecked and incised panels of camels, mounted spearmen, ibex and raiding scenes, interspersed with wusum — the abstract brands each tribe marked on its animals and its territory. A continuous tradition running alongside the written graffiti.
entries.note: Majeed Khan, 'Prehistoric Rock Art of Northern Saudi Arabia' and the Saudi rock-art surveys.

entries.label: The camel and the horse in the plateau's art
entries.hint: The camel dominates the interior's art from the moment it is domesticated for transport and war; the horse appears later and rarer, a marker of status. The rock panels are the visual record of the two animals that defined the society.
entries.note: Khan, Saudi rock-art surveys; the horse's later arrival is discussed in the Arabian equine literature.

entries.label: The huda and the rock-art dancers
entries.loc: the caravan routes of the plateau
entries.hint: The huda — the caravan chant that set the camels' walking pace — is remembered in the later Arabic tradition as immemorial, and files of linked dancing figures appear in the plateau's rock art. The interior's music survives only in these two indirect traces.
entries.note: the Arabic literary tradition on the origins of the huda; the dance panels catalogued in the Saudi rock-art surveys. Flagged as interpretive.

categories.label: Thought
categories.subtitle: The Assyrian archive as the first written history of the interior, the slow decipherment of its rock scripts, and the Arab genealogists' memory of the vanished tribes

entries.label: Nineveh's archive as the first history of Najd
entries.loc: Nineveh · reporting on the Arab tribes
entries.hint: The annals, letters and treaty texts of the Assyrian kings are the only narrative source for the central-Arabian tribes before the classical period — an outside, hostile, self-serving record, but a dated one, and the frame every modern account still uses.
entries.note: Ephʿal, 'The Ancient Arabs' (1982); the relevant royal inscriptions in the RINAP series.

entries.label: Reading the rock scripts of the interior
entries.hint: The Thamudic families of the Ancient North Arabian script have been distinguished and partly read since the 19th century; the ongoing project of recording every legible inscription of the interior is still adding thousands of texts a year.
entries.note: Macdonald, 'Ancient North Arabian', in Woodard (ed.), 'The Ancient Languages of Syria-Palestine and Arabia' (2008); the OCIANA project.

entries.label: The genealogists' ancient Najd
entries.hint: The later Muslim genealogists preserved a deep-time tribal map of the plateau — Tasm and Jadis, the 'vanished Arabs', the homelands of Kindah and the rest — part genuine tradition, part origin-myth, and the only Arabic memory of the interior before the caravan cities.
entries.note: Ibn al-Kalbi's genealogical works; al-Hamdani, Sifat Jazirat al-ʿArab; the critical treatment in Hoyland (2001).

categories.label: Economy
categories.subtitle: A camel-herding, raiding interior sitting astride the routes that linked Yemen to Mesopotamia and the Levant, with oasis farms on its eastern edge

entries.label: The camel-nomad economy
entries.hint: Herding camels for milk, transport and trade, moving between the plateau's seasonal pastures and the oases, and raiding to redistribute stock — this was the economic base of the interior for the whole period and for two millennia after.
entries.note: Ephʿal (1982); the broader literature on Arabian pastoral nomadism.

entries.label: The trans-Arabian cross-routes
entries.loc: al-Aflaj, al-Kharj and the Yamama corridor
entries.hint: Najd sat on the routes linking Yemen to Mesopotamia through the eastern oases and the Gulf, and to the Levant along the western edge the Qedarites taxed. The plateau tribes made a living as carriers, guides and toll-takers on both.
entries.note: Groom, 'Frankincense and Myrrh' (1981) on the eastern route; Ephʿal (1982) on the Qedarite tolls.

entries.label: The oasis farms of al-Yamama
entries.loc: Wadi Hanifa and al-Kharj, Saudi Arabia
entries.hint: Date palms and irrigated grain along Wadi Hanifa and at al-Kharj and al-Aflaj were the settled counterpart to the nomad economy — a food surplus, and a target of both the raid and the tribute collector.
entries.note: the Saudi heritage surveys of al-Yamama; the later Arabic descriptions of the Yamama oases.

entries.label: Camels, incense and captives for the north
entries.loc: the plateau · reaching Nineveh and Babylon
entries.hint: The Assyrian and Babylonian tribute and trade lists record aromatics, camels, gold, precious stones and captured people moving from and through the plateau to the Mesopotamian markets — central Arabia as a supplier, not just a frontier.
entries.note: the Assyrian tribute lists; Ephʿal (1982).

categories.label: Technology
categories.subtitle: The rigid camel saddle that made the plateau tribes a military factor, the deep wells and cisterns of the routes, and the horse and the bow

entries.label: The North Arabian camel saddle
entries.hint: Over this period the plateau tribes moved from riding on a cushion behind the hump to a rigid frame saddle over it, which let a rider fight with spear and bow from camel-back. It is the technology that turned the camel herders into a force outside empires had to reckon with.
entries.note: Richard Bulliet, 'The Camel and the Wheel' (1975), on the North Arabian saddle.

entries.label: Wells, cisterns and the falaj frontier
entries.loc: the routes and the eastern oases
entries.hint: Deep wells and rock-cut cisterns dug and maintained along the routes were what made the plateau crossable; from the east, the qanat or falaj technique of tapping groundwater by tunnel reached the Yamama and al-Aflaj oases.
entries.note: the falaj literature (Wilkinson, 'Water and Society in Oman'); the al-Aflaj name itself preserves the technique.

entries.label: The horse and the composite bow
entries.hint: The horse — expensive to keep in the desert and reserved for the elite — and the composite bow gave the camel-borne tribes a fast strike arm. The pairing of camel for the march and horse for the charge became the classic Arabian way of war.
entries.note: the Arabian equine and archery literature; the horse's spread is later than the camel's and less evenly attested.

categories.label: Exchange
categories.subtitle: Two centuries of dealings with Assyria, a privileged alliance with Persia, a Qedarite king in the politics of Judah, and the plateau as the corridor between the two Fertile Crescents

entries.label: Assyria and the Arabs
entries.hint: Two centuries of tribute, campaign, treaty and hostage exchange between Nineveh and the tribal leaders of the desert edge — the first sustained relationship between a great empire and central Arabia, and the one that put the plateau into history.
entries.note: Ephʿal, 'The Ancient Arabs' (1982); the Assyrian frontier correspondence.

entries.label: Qedar and the Persian Empire
entries.loc: the Egyptian frontier and the northern desert
entries.hint: Under the Achaemenids, Qedar became a privileged ally guarding the approaches to Egypt and the Arabian trade, exempt from tribute and free to tax the caravans. Herodotus records that the Persians never subjected 'the Arabians'.
entries.note: Herodotus III.4–9, 88, 91; Ephʿal (1982).

entries.label: Geshem the Arabian and Judah
entries.hint: The book of Nehemiah names Geshem the Arabian — the Qedarite king — among the leaders opposing the rebuilding of Jerusalem's wall and accusing Nehemiah of planning revolt. The plateau's rulers were players in the provincial politics of the Persian Levant.
entries.note: Nehemiah 2:19, 6:1–6; the identification with Qedar via the Tell el-Maskhuta bowls (Dumbrell 1971).

entries.label: The corridor between the two Fertile Crescents
entries.hint: Najd's routes tied the Yemen of the incense kingdoms to Mesopotamia and to the Mediterranean, and the plateau tribes controlled the wells that made those routes usable — a role central Arabia kept, under every later power, for the next two thousand years.
entries.note: Groom (1981); Hoyland, 'Arabia and the Arabs' (2001).

categories.label: World
categories.subtitle: The camel completes the making of the autonomous desert nomad, and 'Arab' enters the record of the literate empires — the two developments that set the terms for the next 2,500 years

entries.label: The camel and the making of the Arab nomad
entries.hint: The domestication of the dromedary for transport and war, completed in this period, created a mobile, self-supplying desert society that could cross the sands, raid the settled lands and vanish. Every empire from Assyria to the Ottomans would fail to control it.
entries.note: Bulliet, 'The Camel and the Wheel' (1975); Ephʿal (1982).

entries.label: 'Arab' enters history
entries.loc: the desert edge of the Fertile Crescent
entries.hint: From Gindibu in 853 BC the plateau's people are a named, taxed and fought category in the records of the literate empires. Central Arabia's documented history begins not with its own writing but with the writing of its neighbours about it.
entries.note: the Kurkh Monolith; Ephʿal (1982); Hoyland (2001).

entries.label: The thread continues — Qaryat al-Faw and Kindah
entries.loc: Qaryat al-Faw, southern Najd, Saudi Arabia
entries.hint: This folio stops at 300 BC where the Assyrian and Persian records fade. The next centuries bring the caravan city of Qaryat al-Faw at the plateau's southern gate, the rise of the kingdom of Kindah, and central Arabia's entry into the classical world.
entries.note: a forward reference: najd-300bc-632 (Qaryat al-Faw, Kindah and the road to the Ridda) is planned but not yet built.

categories.label: Lives
categories.subtitle: Five ruling queens, the priestesses of the sanctuary, and the captive people counted among the plunder

entries.label: The Arab queens
entries.hint: Zabibe, Samsi, Yatiʿe, Teʾelkhunu and Tabua ruled North Arabian confederations in the 8th and 7th centuries BC — leading armies against Assyria, negotiating tribute, and, in Teʾelkhunu's case, holding priestly office. They are the most prominent women in the ancient history of the peninsula's interior.
entries.note: the Assyrian annals; Ephʿal (1982); Naʾaman on the Arab queens; Hoyland (2001).

entries.label: The priestess and the women of the inscriptions
entries.hint: The apkallatu who kept the gods at Adummatu held real authority in the confederation, and among the rock graffiti of the interior are texts by women — mourning a brother, recording their own journey, naming their own lineage.
entries.note: the Assyrian references to the apkallatu; the women's inscriptions catalogued in OCIANA.

entries.label: The tribute in people
entries.loc: the desert camps · carried to Assyria
entries.hint: The Assyrian campaign accounts list human beings among the plunder taken from the 'Arab' camps, and the plateau's own raiding economy moved captives alongside camels. The enslaved of the ancient interior are counted in the sources and named in almost none of them.
entries.note: the Assyrian campaign inscriptions on Arab captives; Ephʿal (1982).
